content: Sulfamethoxazole inhibits bacterial synthesis of dihydrofolic acid by competing with para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA). Trimethoprim interferes with the production of tetrahydrofolic acid from dihydrofolic acid by binding to and reversibly inhibiting the enzyme dihydrofolate reductase, which is essential for this process. The combination of sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim blocks two sequential steps in the biosynthesis of nucleic acids and proteins that are critical for bacterial survival. In vitro studies have demonstrated that bacterial resistance develops more slowly when sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim are used together compared to when either agent is used alone. Sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim have been shown to be effective against most strains of the following microorganisms, both in vitro and in clinical infections as outlined in the Indications and Usage section: Aerobic Gram-positive microorganisms: Streptococcus pneumoniae Aerobic Gram-negative microorganisms: Escherichia coli (including susceptible enterotoxigenic strains associated with traveler's diarrhea) Klebsiella species Enterobacter species Haemophilus influenzae Morganella morganii Proteus mirabilis Proteus vulgaris Shigella flexneri Shigella sonnei Other organisms: Pneumocystis jirovecii When available, clinical microbiology laboratories should provide in vitro susceptibility test results for antimicrobial drugs used in the hospital to the physician. These reports should include periodic updates on the susceptibility profiles of nosocomial and community-acquired pathogens. Such reports are intended to assist physicians in selecting appropriate antimicrobial therapy. Dilution Techniques: Quantitative methods are used to determine the minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of antimicrobial agents. MICs provide an estimate of the susceptibility of bacteria to specific antimicrobial compounds. These values should be determined using standardized test methods, such as broth or agar dilution. The MIC results should be interpreted based on established criteria. Diffusion Techniques: Quantitative methods that measure the diameter of inhibition zones can also provide reproducible estimates of bacterial susceptibility to antimicrobial agents. Zone sizes should be determined using standardized test methods. A 75 µg trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole disk is used to test the susceptibility of microorganisms to this combination. The interpretive criteria for disk diffusion testing are provided in the relevant guidelines. A report of Susceptible indicates that the antimicrobial agent is likely to inhibit the growth of the pathogen if it achieves the necessary concentrations at the site of infection. A report of Intermediate suggests that the result is equivocal. If the microorganism is not fully susceptible to alternative, clinically feasible drugs, the test should be repeated. This category may have clinical applicability in body sites where the drug is physiologically concentrated or in cases where high doses of the drug can be used. It also provides a buffer zone to account for minor technical variations in testing. A report of Resistant indicates that the antimicrobial agent is unlikely to inhibit the growth of the pathogen at concentrations typically achievable at the infection site. Alternative therapy should be considered. Quality Control: Standardized susceptibility testing procedures require the use of laboratory controls to ensure the accuracy and precision of the supplies, reagents, and techniques used in the assay. These controls also monitor the performance of the individuals conducting the tests. Standard trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole powder should yield MIC values within the specified range. Similarly, a 75 µg trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole disk should meet the established criteria for zone sizes.
